To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peripheral IGF system is altered in ALS, but not in multiple sclerosis.
serum levels of insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I) and insulin are reduced in patients with amyotropic lateral sclerosis, whereas serum levels of IGF-I binding proteins (IGFBPs) are increased.

ALS patients have significantly reduced levels of circulating insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and significantly increased levels of IGF-binding proteins 1, 2, and 3, whereas multiple sclerosis (MS) patients do not show significant changes in the IGF-1 trophic system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral scleroses (ALS) and other neurological disorders.
the role of the IGF system in the peripheral nervous system, with special reference to the trophic support of spinal motor neurons in ALS and of oligodendroglia in multiple sclerosis.
a possible role of the peripheral IGC-I system in the development and/or progression of ALS and multiple sclerosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ALS patients show a reduced IGF-I level and an increase in IGF-binding proteins.
the IGF system is not a good marker of ALS.
the peripheral IGF system is not affected in multiple sclerosis, while it is affected in amyotrophic sclerosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ALS and MS patients show a significant reduction of circulating IGFs.
the IGF-I system is not involved in MS, but it is in ALS.
IGF-I is reduced in ALS and that this may be due to a reduced production of IGF-I in ALS patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ALS patients may have an impaired IGF-I system that is not present in multiple sclerosis.
ALS patients show significant changes in the IGF-binding proteins.
the peripheral IGF system is involved in the pathogenesis of ALS and that it may represent a potential target for therapeutic interventions.
